```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
parks <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1JNbcHQvKfm4menXhUjP71sYF207Y8ozm", quiet = TRUE)
```

## Part 1: Walkthrough {#walkthrough}

This is not a coding class, but we will use R for our data analysis. You don't need to write code from scratch. You do need to find your way around RStudio and change code that I give you. R is a free programming language that is very good at analyzing and mapping spatial data, and RStudio is the program we use to work in R.

### Step 1: Install R and RStudio

::: {.why}
Install both programs: [download R](https://cran.rstudio.com/) (pick the version for your operating system) and [download RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/). Then open RStudio and change one setting. You only need to do this once.
:::

Go to **Tools** \> **Global Options**, uncheck "Restore .RData into workspace at startup", and choose **Never** for "Save workspace to .RData on exit".

### Step 2: Find the Four Panes

::: {.why}
RStudio has four panes. You write and run code in **Source**. **Console** runs one command at a time and saves nothing, so it is good for quick tests. **Environment** lists the objects you have made, and **Output** shows plots, maps and files.
:::

![RStudio Panes](images/rstudio-panes-labeled.jpeg){fig-alt="The RStudio window divided into four labeled panes: Source at top left with an R script open, Console at bottom left showing the same commands after they ran, Environment at top right listing the object mpg_plot, and Output at bottom right showing a scatter plot."}

### Step 3: Install the Packages

::: {.why}
Packages add tools to R. Install them once, by pasting these lines into the **Console** one at a time. After that, you only load them with `library()`, and I will always tell you which ones to load.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("tidyverse")  #data analysis and ggplot2 graphics
install.packages("sf")         #spatial data
install.packages("tmap")       #maps
install.packages("maptiles")   #basemaps
install.packages("gt")         #tables
install.packages("e1071")      #skewness and other statistics
install.packages("car")        #statistical tests such as Levene's test
install.packages("terra")      #rasters
install.packages("stars")      #rasters and other gridded data
install.packages("sp")         #older spatial data tools
install.packages("sfdep")      #centrography and spdep tools for sf data
install.packages("spdep")      #neighbors and spatial autocorrelation
install.packages("spatialreg") #spatial regression
install.packages("spatstat")   #point pattern analysis
install.packages("gstat")      #interpolation and kriging
install.packages("GWmodel")    #geographically weighted regression
install.packages("tigris")     #census boundaries
install.packages("deldir")     #Voronoi polygons
install.packages("cols4all")   #color palettes
```

### Step 4: Open the Template and Run It

::: {.why}
An R Markdown file (.Rmd) holds text and code together. Code goes in **chunks**, and each chunk should do one task. [Download the class template (.Rmd)](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1t6PT4vNp1e1e10PDcEfOrQp9c9m8bVIu) and save it in a GEOG391 folder, not in Downloads. To start your own later, use **File** \> **New File** \> **R Markdown**.
:::

Open the template, change the header to your name and today's date, and click the green arrow on the second chunk to run it. It loads the packages and the data on the 16 parks in Chapel Hill. `parks` then appears in the Environment pane, and double-clicking it opens it as a table.

![](images/run_codechunk.png){fig-alt="An .Rmd open in RStudio. Labels point to the Add Code Chunk button in the toolbar, the set up chunk, the green Run Code Chunk arrow at the right edge of the library and data chunk, and the parks object (16 obs. of 18 variables) that appears in the Environment pane after the chunk runs."}

![](images/view_object.png){fig-alt="The parks data opened as a table in RStudio, with 16 rows and columns OBJECTID, Park_Name, Address, Zipcode, Park_Hours and Rental_Opportunities. The first row is Homestead Park, 100 Northern Park Dr, Chapel Hill NC, 27516, Dawn to 10pm, Yes."}

### Step 5: Make a Map and Knit

::: {.why}
Add a new chunk with the **+C** button and put the code below in it. Start every command with a comment (`#`) that says what it does. Then click **Knit** to turn the .Rmd into an .html file with your text, code and output. The .html is saved in the same folder as the .Rmd.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#map the parks in Chapel Hill, colored by their hours
tm_shape(parks) + tm_dots("Park_Hours", size = 0.8)
```

![](images/clipboard-2379786468.png){fig-alt="RStudio after running the chunks. Each comment line (load libraries, load data, create a map of parks in Chapel Hill) is boxed and labeled Comments. Below the last chunk is a map of park points in Chapel Hill colored by Park_Hours, with a legend listing 6-10pm, Dawn to 10pm, Dawn to 11pm, Dawn to Dusk, Public Space: 24hrs and Unknown."}

![](images/knit.png){fig-alt="The RStudio toolbar for r_practice.Rmd with the Knit button, a ball of yarn icon next to the word Knit, outlined in red."}

The bottom of the template shows how to make headings, **bold** and *italic* text, and the chunk options that hide code (`echo = FALSE`) or hide everything (`include = FALSE`).

## Part 2: Partner Practice {#partner-practice}

Both partners work in their own copy of the template. Partner A maps which parks have playground equipment (`Playground_Equipment`), and Partner B maps which parks have trails (`Trails`). Each task tells you in parentheses which walkthrough step to reuse.

:::: {.partners}
::: {.partner .partner-a}
### Partner A: Playgrounds

1. Run the template's data chunk, and open `parks` as a table. *(Step 4)*
2. In a new chunk with a comment, map the parks colored by `Playground_Equipment`. *(Step 5)*
3. In another chunk, count the parks with and without playground equipment with `table(parks$Playground_Equipment)`.
4. Add a second-level heading and one sentence about your map, hide the code of your map chunk with `echo = FALSE`, and knit. *(Step 5)*

When you finish, bring your knitted .html and the names of the parks with playground equipment to Part 3.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B: Trails

1. Run the template's data chunk, and open `parks` as a table. *(Step 4)*
2. In a new chunk with a comment, map the parks colored by `Trails`. *(Step 5)*
3. In another chunk, count the parks with and without trails with `table(parks$Trails)`.
4. Add a second-level heading and one sentence about your map, hide the code of your map chunk with `echo = FALSE`, and knit. *(Step 5)*

When you finish, bring your knitted .html and the names of the parks with trails to Part 3.
:::
::::

## Part 3: Together {#together}

1. Open both knitted files side by side. Check that each one hides the map code but still shows the map.
2. Which parks have both playground equipment and trails?
3. Where in town are those parks?

::: {.deliver}
Each pair turns in one index card before leaving. Write both of your names on it, the number of parks with playground equipment and the number with trails, and the names of the parks that have both.
:::

## Answer Key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
n_play <- sum(parks$Playground_Equipment == "Yes")
n_trail <- sum(parks$Trails == "Yes")
both <- parks$Park_Name[parks$Playground_Equipment == "Yes" & parks$Trails == "Yes"]
```

`r n_play` of the `r nrow(parks)` parks have playground equipment and `r n_trail` have trails. The parks with both are `r knitr::combine_words(both)`. They are spread across town: Cedar Falls Park in the north off Weaver Dairy Road, the Chapel Hill Community Center on Estes Drive near the middle, and Southern Community Park in the south.

A good knitted file has the map but not the map code, a second-level heading above it, and a sentence describing the map.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#### Partner A ####
#map the parks, colored by whether they have playground equipment
tm_shape(parks) + tm_dots("Playground_Equipment", size = 0.8)

#count the parks with and without playground equipment
table(parks$Playground_Equipment)

#### Partner B ####
#map the parks, colored by whether they have trails
tm_shape(parks) + tm_dots("Trails", size = 0.8)

#count the parks with and without trails
table(parks$Trails)

#### Together ####
#parks with both
parks |> filter(Playground_Equipment == "Yes", Trails == "Yes") |> pull(Park_Name)
```

A map chunk with its code hidden starts with `{r, echo = FALSE}` instead of `{r}`.
